turns.doctor_question: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah. Well, honestly, I’ve been putting off making this appointment for a really long time, but... what finally scared me into actually coming in today is what's been happening at my job. I work in television and film as a camera operator and an editor, so I’m constantly dealing with a lot of media and juggling a million little technical details. And lately, I just keep making these really, really dumb technical mistakes. Mistakes I absolutely know better than to make. 

Like, I’ll be on a shoot, right? And we're moving fast, swapping out media, and I will end up labeling the camera cards wrong before handing them off. Do you know how much of a nightmare that is for the post-production team to sort out? Or when I'm in the edit bay, I'll be going through the director's notes and I'll just completely miss a timecode note. Just skip right over it as if it wasn't even written there. 

The one that really broke the camel's back, though, was the other day. I was exporting a cut for a client—which, you know, takes a long time to render and upload—and I sent it off with the completely wrong lower-third graphic on the screen. And the worst part is, I checked it! I literally sat there, watched the export, thought I verified everything, and I still missed it. It’s just so embarrassing and terrifying because I have my bachelor's in this, I've been doing it for years, and I shouldn't be making these kinds of careless rookie errors when I know exactly how to do my job. It just makes me look so unprofessional, and I can't figure out why I keep doing it.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless, 'rookie' technical errors at work, such as mislabeling camera cards and missing timecode notes, despite knowing better and checking their work.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have similar difficulties with focus or careless mistakes when you were growing up in school?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh, school. Yeah, I mean... it’s funny you ask that because I was just thinking about my childhood when I was trying to work up the nerve to make this appointment. School was... well, it was a lot. I don't know if it was always careless mistakes with the work itself, necessarily, but I was definitely a massive handful for the teachers. 

Like, even way back in elementary school—I vividly remember third grade, I had this teacher, Mrs. Gable, and she actually had to physically move my desk away from the other kids. She put me right up next to her desk at the very front of the room, kind of on an island by myself. And it wasn't because I didn't know the material, it was just... I literally could not stay in my seat. I was always popping up to go look at the class pet, or wandering over to the trash can, or I'd be leaning over tapping the kid next to me, just completely bothering my classmates. 

And the blurting! Oh my god, the blurting out. A teacher would ask a question to the class and I wouldn't even raise my hand, the answer would just fly out of my mouth. Or I'd finish someone else's sentence. It was like there was zero filter between my brain and my mouth, and the craziest part is that I honestly wouldn't even realize I was doing it until the teacher was already reprimanding me or telling me to sit down and be quiet. It was just this automatic impulse. So, yeah, it was always a whole production, just constantly getting my seating arrangement changed because I couldn't just sit still and be quiet like everyone else.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they could not stay in their seat and were always popping up or wandering around the classroom.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient describes blurting out answers in class before raising their hand.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions finishing other people's sentences and tapping or bothering classmates, indicating interrupting and intruding on others.

turns.doctor_question: Nowadays as an adult, do you still feel physically restless or have trouble sitting still for long periods?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, 100 percent. It’s... it’s honestly exhausting because you'd think as a 38-year-old professional I would have grown out of that by now, but I really haven't. It just looks a little different now than wandering over to the class pet like I did in third grade. 

Now, it's... well, a perfect example is when we do client screenings. When we finally have a cut ready and the directors or the corporate clients come into the edit bay to watch it down... they usually have these really nice, plush couches set up in the back of the room, right? And the lights are dimmed, and everyone is just quietly watching the monitors. And as the editor, my job in that exact moment is literally just to sit in my chair, hit the spacebar to play the video, and watch quietly with them. 

But sitting still through a client screening like that... it literally feels like there is this intense pressure building up right under my skin. Like this physical buzzing or humming. I'll be sitting there, and my brain is just screaming at me that I need to get up, I need to pace, I need to go grab a water, I need to do *something* with my body. And I know, logically, I know I’m supposed to just sit there and watch quietly, but it takes every ounce of my willpower to not just jump out of the chair. I end up shifting my weight a million times, bouncing my leg under the desk where they hopefully can't see it, or like, picking at my cuticles. Sometimes I'll even pretend I need to check a cable connection behind the monitors just so I have an excuse to stand up for ten seconds. It's just this constant, uncomfortable need to move, even when the situation completely, absolutely demands that I don't.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes shifting their weight constantly, bouncing their leg under the desk, and picking at their cuticles while trying to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits to making up excuses, like checking a cable connection, just to stand up and leave their seat during client screenings where they are expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly confirms feeling physically restless, describing it as an intense pressure building under the skin and a constant, uncomfortable need to move.
